{{Short description|Type of metric space}}In [[metric geometry]], an '''injective metric space''', or equivalently a '''hyperconvex metric space''', is a [[metric space]] with certain properties generalizing those of the [[real line]] and of [[Chebyshev distance|L<sub>∞</sub> distances]] in higher-[[dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[vector space]]s. These properties can be defined in two seemingly different ways: hyperconvexity involves the intersection properties of [[ball (mathematics)|closed balls]] in the space, while injectivity involves the [[isometry|isometric embeddings]] of the space into larger spaces. However it is a theorem of {{harvtxt|Aronszajn|Panitchpakdi|1956}} that these two different types of definitions are equivalent.<ref>See e.g. {{harvnb|Chepoi|1997}}.</ref>

== Hyperconvexity ==

A metric space <math>X</math> is said to be '''hyperconvex''' if it is [[convex metric|convex]] and its [[ball (mathematics)|closed balls]] have the binary [[Helly family|Helly property]]. That is:
#Any two points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> can be connected by the [[isometry|isometric]] image of a line segment of length equal to the distance between the points (i.e. <math>X</math> is a path space).
#If <math>F</math> is any family of closed balls <math display=block>{\bar B}_r(p) = \{q \mid d(p,q) \le r\}</math> such that each pair of balls in <math>F</math> meets, then there exists a point <math>x</math> common to all the balls in <math>F</math>. 
Equivalently, a metric space <math>X</math> is hyperconvex if, for any set of points <math>p_i</math> in <math>X</math> and radii <math>r_i>0</math> satisfying <math>r_i+r_j\ge d(p_i,p_j)</math> for each <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>, there is a point <math>q</math> in <math>X</math> that is within distance <math>r_i</math> of each <math>p_i</math> (that is, <math>d(p_i,q) \le r_i</math> for all <math>i</math>).

== Injectivity ==
{{See also|Retraction (topology)}}
A [[retract (metric geometry)|retraction]] of a metric space <math>X</math> is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f</math> mapping <math>X</math> to a subspace of itself, such that
# for all <math>x \in X</math> we have that <math>f(f(x))=f(x)</math>; that is, <math>f</math> is the [[identity function]] on its image (i.e. it is [[idempotent]]), and
# for all <math>x, y \in X</math> we have that <math>d(f(x),f(y))\le d(x,y)</math>; that is, <math>f</math> is [[nonexpansive mapping|nonexpansive]].
A ''retract'' of a space <math>X</math> is a subspace of <math>X</math> that is an image of a retraction.
A metric space <math>X</math> is said to be '''injective''' if, whenever <math>X</math> is [[isometry|isometric]] to a subspace <math>Z</math> of a space <math>Y</math>, that subspace <math>Z</math> is a retract of <math>Y</math>.

== Examples ==

Examples of hyperconvex metric spaces include
* The real line
* <math>\R^d</math> with the [[Lp space|<math>\ell</math><sup>∞</sup> distance]]
* [[taxicab geometry|Manhattan distance]] (''L''<sub>1</sub>) in the plane (which is equivalent up to rotation and scaling to the ''L''<sub>∞</sub>), but not in higher dimensions
* The [[tight span]] of a metric space
* Any complete [[real tree]]
* <math>\operatorname{Aim}(X)</math> &ndash; see [[Metric space aimed at its subspace]]
Due to the equivalence between hyperconvexity and injectivity, these spaces are all also injective.

== Properties ==

In an injective space, the radius of the [[circumradius|minimum ball]] that contains any set <math>S</math> is equal to half the [[diameter]] of <math>S</math>. This follows since the balls of radius half the diameter, centered at the points of <math>S</math>, intersect pairwise and therefore by hyperconvexity have a common intersection; a ball of radius half the diameter centered at a point of this common intersection contains all of <math>S</math>. Thus, injective spaces satisfy a particularly strong form of [[Jung's theorem]].

Every injective space is a [[complete space]],{{sfn|Aronszajn|Panitchpakdi|1956}} and every [[metric map]] (or, equivalently, [[short map|nonexpansive mapping, or short map]]) on a bounded injective space has a [[Fixed-point theorem|fixed point]].<ref>{{harvnb|Sine|1979}}; {{harvnb|Soardi|1979}}.</ref> A metric space is injective [[if and only if]] it is an [[injective object]] in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of [[category of metric spaces|metric spaces and metric maps]].<ref>For additional properties of injective spaces see {{harvnb|Espínola|Khamsi|2001}}.</ref>
